performers: Carol Brice, contralto; Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra; Fritz Reiner
intro: Fritz Reiner and the Pittsburgh Symphony recorded all thirteen numbers of Falla’s ballet El amor brujo, with the contralto Carol Brice, in February 1946. The Ritual Fire Dance is on side three of the six-side Columbia set.

sections.label: Intro · Scene, the cave and a love-song
A · The ghost, terror, magic circle
B · Midnight and Ritual Fire Dance
C · Scene and song of the will-o’-the-wisp
E · Dance of the Game of Love

cues.title: Thirteen numbers on six sides
cues.text: Falla’s complete ballet takes up six 78-rpm sides, with its thirteen numbers spread across them. The contralto Carol Brice sings on sides 1, 4 and 6. Midnight and the Ritual Fire Dance are on side 3.
cues.evidence: The Internet Archive item for Columbia set MM-633 lists the numbers on each side (side 1: Nos. 1–3; side 2: Nos. 4–6; side 3: Nos. 7–8; side 4: Nos. 9–10; side 5: No. 11; side 6: Nos. 12–13) and credits Carol Brice only on sides 1, 4 and 6. https://archive.org/details/mm-633-falla-el-amor-brujo

cues.title: Side one, Nos. 1–3
cues.text: Side one ends with the contralto’s Song of the sorrows of love, No. 3, after the Introduction and Scene and In the cave at night.
cues.evidence: Side 1 of Columbia set MM-633 carries No. 1, Introduction and Scene; No. 2, In the cave at night; No. 3, Song of the sorrows of love, and Brice is credited on it. https://archive.org/details/mm-633-falla-el-amor-brujo

cues.title: The apparition and Dance of Terror
cues.text: The dead husband’s ghost appears. In the Dance of Terror that follows, he frightens Candelas and her new lover Carmelo, and the music becomes fast and rhythmic.
cues.evidence: John Henken’s note for the Los Angeles Philharmonic: in the final version the ghost first frightens the couple in the Dance of Terror. Side 2 of the Columbia set carries No. 4, The apparition, and No. 5, Dance of Terror. https://www.laphil.com/works/el-amor-brujo https://archive.org/details/mm-633-falla-el-amor-brujo

cues.title: Gitanería for Pastora Imperio, 1915
cues.text: The first version was a gitanería with songs, dances and spoken text, written around the dancer Pastora Imperio, whose mother suggested an old Andalusian legend. On the day of the première, 15 April 1915, Falla told a Madrid paper that he and his collaborators had produced a new, unusual work, one they had “felt”.
cues.evidence: John Henken, Los Angeles Philharmonic note: the work was requested by Pastora Imperio, whose mother, Rosario la Mejorana, suggested the legend; première at the Teatro Lara, Madrid, April 1915. The Archivo Manuel de Falla page “1915, a busy year” gives the première as 15 April 1915 and quotes Falla’s interview in La Patria (Rafael Benedito), which it places in that day’s issue and footnotes as 16 April; Falla speaks before the audience’s verdict (“we don’t know what effect it will produce”). https://www.laphil.com/works/el-amor-brujo https://www.manueldefalla.com/en/1915-a-busy-year

cues.title: Ritual Fire Dance
cues.text: Candelas dances to exorcise the ghost. The Chester piano edition of 1921 carries the subtitle “pour chasser les mauvais esprits” (to drive away evil spirits).
cues.evidence: J. & W. Chester, Danse rituelle du feu, piano edition (1921), printed page 1: “Danse rituelle du feu (pour chasser les mauvais esprits)”, Allegro ma non troppo. John Henken’s note: Candelas tries to exorcise the ghost in the Ritual Fire Dance. https://archive.org/details/danserituelleduf00fall https://www.laphil.com/works/el-amor-brujo
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Carol Brice, Pittsburgh, 1946
cues.text: Carol Brice, born in Sedalia, North Carolina, in 1918, was the first Black musician to win the Naumburg Award, in 1944. She recorded the ballet with Reiner at the Syria Mosque on 5 February 1946.
cues.evidence: Naumburg Foundation, biography of Carol Brice (first black musician to win the Naumburg award, 1944; born 16 April 1918, Sedalia, North Carolina). Recording date and venue from the Internet Archive item and Sony’s notes for the box set containing the recording. https://www.naumburg.org/naumburg-winners/carol-brice https://archive.org/details/mm-633-falla-el-amor-brujo

cues.title: Side four, Nos. 9 and 10
cues.text: Side four holds a short scene, then the contralto’s Song of the will-o’-the-wisp. Roger Nichols compared it to Carmen: “love is not to be caught”. Meanwhile Lucía draws the ghost away from the lovers.
cues.evidence: Roger Nichols, booklet note for Garrick Ohlsson’s Falla recital (Hyperion CDA68177): the Canción del fuego fatuo — “as in Carmen, love is not to be caught”. Los Angeles Philharmonic note: Lucía seduces the ghost while the lovers kiss. Side 4 of the Columbia set carries No. 9, Scene, and No. 10, Song of the will-o’-the-wisp. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA68177 https://www.laphil.com/works/el-amor-brujo

cues.title: Pantomima in 7/8
cues.text: The Pantomima, No. 11, takes up a whole side of the set. It is in an asymmetric 7/8 as the ghost’s power wanes. In 1959 Poulenc based the third of his Novelettes for piano on its theme.
cues.evidence: Roger Nichols, Hyperion booklet note: in the Pantomima “the spirit’s power is heard to wane, as suggested by the asymmetric 7/8 metre (in 1959 Poulenc would base his third Novelette on this theme)”. IMSLP lists Novelette No. 3 as “sur un thème de Manuel de Falla tiré de El amor brujo”. Side 5 of the Columbia set carries No. 11 alone. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA68177 https://imslp.org/wiki/3_Novelettes,_FP_47/173_(Poulenc,_Francis)

cues.title: Dance of the Game of Love
cues.text: While Lucía distracts the ghost, Candelas and Carmelo exchange the kiss of perfect love. They then mock the ghost in the final number, the Dance of the Game of Love.
cues.evidence: John Henken’s note for the Los Angeles Philharmonic: the ghost is distracted by Lucía, Candelas and Carmelo kiss “and then mock the ghost in the final dance (Dance of the Game of Love)”. https://www.laphil.com/works/el-amor-brujo

cues.title: Finale: Morning bells
cues.text: The finale, the bells of dawn (“campanas del amanecer”), closes the ballet. The contralto is heard again on the final side.
cues.evidence: Side 6 of Columbia set MM-633 carries No. 12, Dance of the game of love, and No. 13, Finale: Morning bells, with Brice credited (Internet Archive item). Columbia’s 1954 Spanish catalogue titles the last number “Final. Campanas del amanecer”. https://archive.org/details/mm-633-falla-el-amor-brujo https://www.eresbil.eus/web/uploads/archivosGeneradorWeb/Catalogos/erelib_NL0212CAT_01_v.pdf

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Carol Brice (contralto), Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra (orchestra), Fritz Reiner (conductor)
fields.note: Carol Brice is credited only on sides 1, 4 and 6. Individual orchestral players are not identified.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: The ballet in thirteen numbers, recorded on six 78-rpm sides
fields.note: The thirteen numbers are listed side by side on the Columbia set and match the number sequence of the ballet version; the performing edition used by the orchestra is unknown.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Both the Internet Archive item and Sony’s box-set notes give 5 February 1946. The same notes record other sessions of 2 and 4 February 1946 for other works.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: The Pittsburgh Symphony’s regular recording venue in these sessions.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: 78-rpm album set; the set was reissued on a ten-inch LP, ML 2006, in 1948.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: M-633 (78s 12409-D to 12411-D); automatic sequence MM-633 (12412-D to 12414-D)
fields.note: The Internet Archive item is labelled MM-633.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: The Internet Archive item and Sony’s notes give the same matrix numbers and side contents.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The item sits in the Internet Archive’s shellackophile-recordings collection; no personal mastering credit is given.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The item was uploaded on 1 April 2022; the date of the transfer itself is not stated.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: Equipment, equalisation and restoration settings are not stated. The file is a single continuous MP3 of the six sides.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Falla died on 14 November 1946. Spanish law protects the works of authors who died before 7 December 1987 for life plus 80 years, so his music remains protected in Spain until the end of 2026; arrangements and modern editions carry their own rights
fields.note: A phonogram term assessment does not clear the composition, an arrangement or a modern score edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU phonogram public-domain basis: commercial publication in 1947, before 1963
fields.note: The project’s eu-published-before-1963 rule applied to a Columbia set issued in 1947 (the Internet Archive item says March 1947, Sony’s notes 24 February 1947, Discogs 1947). This is a territorial phonogram basis, not US or worldwide clearance and not a Creative Commons licence.

composer.epithet: Composer from Cádiz who studied in Paris with Dukas and Debussy and is known for bringing Andalusian song and the guitar into orchestral music.
facts: Piano with José Tragó in Madrid (first prize, 1899); composition with Felipe Pedrell from 1901
Guided by Paul Dukas and Debussy; friends with Albéniz, Ravel and Ricardo Viñes
Gregorio Martínez Sierra and María Lejárraga · Diaghilev and Massine · Picasso · Lorca
An opera, a gitanería and a ballet, a nocturne for piano and orchestra, songs, a puppet opera and a harpsichord concerto; Atlántida unfinished

quote.text: For everything that concerns my trade, my homeland is Paris.
quote.source: Falla to Ignacio Zuloaga, Granada, 12 February 1923; Archivo Manuel de Falla

composer.background:
As a boy in Cádiz, Manuel de Falla ran an imaginary city called Colón. It had a council, newspapers and a theatre, and according to Roland-Manuel’s 1930 biography the great success of the day there was El conde de Villamediana, an opera seria composed and conducted by a certain Manuel de Falla. He kept the game going for six years. Falla was born on 23 November 1876 at 3 Plaza de Mina, and he first intended to be a writer. He told Roland-Manuel in 1928 that at seventeen a conviction at once timid and deep had turned him towards composition.

In Madrid he studied the piano with José Tragó and won the conservatoire’s first prize in 1899. Two years later he asked the Catalan musicologist Felipe Pedrell to teach him; from Pedrell, he told his biographer Jaime Pahissa, came the clearest and most solid guidance for his work.
